claim: The recycling of neurotransmitters is essential for sustained synaptic transmission.
source: The recycling of neurotransmitters is essential for sustained synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a general statement about neurotransmitter recycling supported by established scientific knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: In Drosophila, histamine recycling is required for visual synaptic transmission.
source: In Drosophila, histamine recycling is required for visual synaptic transmission.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in Drosophila neurobiology and is referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic histamine is rapidly taken up by laminar glia.
source: Synaptic histamine is rapidly taken up by laminar glia, and is converted to carcinine.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and is part of the established histamine recycling pathway.

claim: Histamine taken up by laminar glia is converted to carcinine.
source: Synaptic histamine is rapidly taken up by laminar glia, and is converted to carcinine.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and is part of the established histamine recycling pathway.

claim: Carcinine is delivered back to photoreceptors after being synthesized in laminar glia.
source: After delivered back to photoreceptors, carcinine is hydrolyzed to release histamine and β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on the histamine recycling pathway.

claim: Carcinine is hydrolyzed in photoreceptors to release histamine and β-alanine.
source: After delivered back to photoreceptors, carcinine is hydrolyzed to release histamine and β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on the Tan hydrolase enzyme.

claim: Histamine released from carcinine hydrolysis is repackaged into synaptic vesicles.
source: This histamine is repackaged into synaptic vesicles, but it is unclear how the β-alanine is returned to the laminar glial cells.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on histamine recycling.

claim: The mechanism by which β-alanine is returned to laminar glial cells was unclear prior to this study.
source: This histamine is repackaged into synaptic vesicles, but it is unclear how the β-alanine is returned to the laminar glial cells.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: A new β-alanine transporter named BalaT was identified in this study.
source: Here, we identified a new β-alanine transporter, which we named BalaT (Beta-alanine Transporter).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Null balat mutants exhibited lower levels of β-alanine.
source: Null balat mutants exhibited lower levels of β-alanine, as well as less β-alanine accumulation in the retina.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS measurements presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Null balat mutants exhibited less β-alanine accumulation in the retina.
source: Null balat mutants exhibited lower levels of β-alanine, as well as less β-alanine accumulation in the retina.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 5D and F.

claim: BalaT is expressed in retinal pigment cells.
source: Moreover, BalaT is expressed and required in retinal pigment cells for maintaining visual synaptic transmission and phototaxis behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the balat-mcherry knock-in experiments shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: BalaT is required in retinal pigment cells for maintaining visual synaptic transmission.
source: Moreover, BalaT is expressed and required in retinal pigment cells for maintaining visual synaptic transmission and phototaxis behavior.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: BalaT is required in retinal pigment cells for maintaining phototaxis behavior.
source: Moreover, BalaT is expressed and required in retinal pigment cells for maintaining visual synaptic transmission and phototaxis behavior.
evidence: This is supported by phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: This study provides the first genetic evidence that retinal pigment cells play a critical role in visual neurotransmission.
source: These results provide the first genetic evidence that retinal pigment cells play a critical role in visual neurotransmission, and suggest that a BalaT-dependent β-alanine trafficking pathway is required for histamine homeostasis and visual neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by the tissue-specific rescue experiments and localization data.

claim: A BalaT-dependent β-alanine trafficking pathway is required for histamine homeostasis.
source: These results provide the first genetic evidence that retinal pigment cells play a critical role in visual neurotransmission, and suggest that a BalaT-dependent β-alanine trafficking pathway is required for histamine homeostasis and visual neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by the reduced histamine levels in balat mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A BalaT-dependent β-alanine trafficking pathway is required for visual neurotransmission.
source: These results provide the first genetic evidence that retinal pigment cells play a critical role in visual neurotransmission, and suggest that a BalaT-dependent β-alanine trafficking pathway is required for histamine homeostasis and visual neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by the loss of ERG transients in balat mutants shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Efficient clearance of neurotransmitters from the synaptic cleft is crucial for terminating a synaptic signal.
source: Efficient clearance of neurotransmitters from the synaptic cleft is crucial for terminating a synaptic signal.
evidence: This is a general principle in neuroscience supported by established knowledge.

claim: Cleared neurotransmitters must be recycled for sustained synaptic transmission to maintain stable levels of transmitters.
source: These cleared neurotransmitters must then be recycled for sustained synaptic transmission (i.e., to maintain stable levels of transmitters) (Blakely and Edwards, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blakely and Edwards, 2012.

claim: Neurons that utilize histamine as a neurotransmitter play important roles in cognition, sleep, and metabolism.
source: Neurons that utilize histamine as a neurotransmitter play important roles in a variety of biological processes, including cognition, sleep, and metabolism, and dysfunction of the histaminergic system in the brain has been linked to multiple neurological diseases (Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 2008 and Panula and Nuutinen, 2013.

claim: Dysfunction of the histaminergic system in the brain has been linked to multiple neurological diseases.
source: Neurons that utilize histamine as a neurotransmitter play important roles in a variety of biological processes, including cognition, sleep, and metabolism, and dysfunction of the histaminergic system in the brain has been linked to multiple neurological diseases (Haas et al., 2008; Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 2008 and Panula and Nuutinen, 2013.

claim: Histamine is particularly important in the Drosophila visual system.
source: Histamine is particularly important in the Drosophila visual system (Hardie, 1989), and histamine recycling is the dominant pathway for maintaining adequate levels of histamine in adult photoreceptors (Borycz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hardie, 1989.

claim: Histamine recycling is the dominant pathway for maintaining adequate levels of histamine in adult photoreceptors.
source: Histamine is particularly important in the Drosophila visual system (Hardie, 1989), and histamine recycling is the dominant pathway for maintaining adequate levels of histamine in adult photoreceptors (Borycz et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borycz et al., 2002.

claim: The histamine recycling process involves both neurons and glial cells that surround the synapse in Drosophila and mammalian systems.
source: In this system, and in mammalian systems as well, the histamine recycling process involves both neurons and glial cells that surround the synapse (Edwards and Meinertzhagen, 2010; Yoshikawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edwards and Meinertzhagen, 2010 and Yoshikawa et al., 2013.

claim: A network of glia cells and pigment cells interconnected via gap junctions plays a key role in the long-distance recycling of histamine in the Drosophila visual system.
source: In fact, a network of glia cells and pigment cells interconnected via gap junctions plays a key role in the long-distance recycling of histamine in the Drosophila visual system (Chaturvedi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaturvedi et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanisms by which the cellular network recycles histamine and its metabolites were unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the mechanisms by which this cellular network recycles histamine and its metabolites are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Histamine released by photoreceptors into the optic lamina is quickly removed from the synaptic cleft by epithelia glial cells.
source: Once histamine is released by a photoreceptor into the optic lamina, it is quickly removed from the synaptic cleft by epithelia glial cells that surround the synapse.
evidence: This is supported by prior research on histamine recycling.

claim: In laminar glia, histamine is conjugated to β-alanine by Ebony to form carcinine.
source: In these laminar glia, histamine is conjugated to β-alanine by an N-β-alanyl-dopamine synthase, called Ebony, to form the inactive metabolite, carcinine (Borycz et al., 2002; Richardt et al., 2003, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2002 and Richardt et al., 2002, 2003.

claim: Ebony is an N-β-alanyl-dopamine synthase.
source: In these laminar glia, histamine is conjugated to β-alanine by an N-β-alanyl-dopamine synthase, called Ebony, to form the inactive metabolite, carcinine (Borycz et al., 2002; Richardt et al., 2003, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2002 and Richardt et al., 2002, 2003.

claim: Carcinine is an inactive metabolite of histamine.
source: In these laminar glia, histamine is conjugated to β-alanine by an N-β-alanyl-dopamine synthase, called Ebony, to form the inactive metabolite, carcinine (Borycz et al., 2002; Richardt et al., 2003, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2002 and Richardt et al., 2002, 2003.

claim: CarT is a carcinine transporter responsible for the uptake of carcinine from the synaptic cleft into photoreceptors.
source: Recently, a carcinine transporter, CarT that is responsible for the uptake of carcinine from the synaptic cleft into photoreceptors has been identified (Chaturvedi et al., 2016; Stenesen et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chaturvedi et al., 2016, Stenesen et al., 2015, and Xu et al., 2015.

claim: CarT retrieves carcinine directly from the laminar synaptic cleft, indicating that carcinine is not transported from laminar glia to photoreceptor cell bodies through a long-distance trafficking mechanism.
source: The discovery that CarT retrieves carcinine directly from the laminar synaptic cleft indicates that carcinine is not transported from laminar glia to photoreceptor cell bodies through a long-distance trafficking mechanism involving the laminar glial and pigment cell network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discovery of CarT and its localization.

claim: Within photoreceptors, carcinine is hydrolyzed by Tan to generate histamine and β-alanine.
source: Within photoreceptors, carcinine is hydrolyzed to generate histamine and β-alanine, a reaction catalyzed by an N-β-alanyl-dopamine hydrolase called Tan (Borycz et al., 2002; True et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2002 and True et al., 2005.

claim: Tan is an N-β-alanyl-dopamine hydrolase.
source: Within photoreceptors, carcinine is hydrolyzed to generate histamine and β-alanine, a reaction catalyzed by an N-β-alanyl-dopamine hydrolase called Tan (Borycz et al., 2002; True et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2002 and True et al., 2005.

claim: Regenerated histamine from carcinine hydrolysis is repackaged into synaptic vesicles for subsequent light-induced release.
source: This regenerated histamine is then repackaged into synaptic vesicles for subsequent light-induced release, but it is unclear how β-alanine is returned to the laminar glial cells (where it is needed to inactivate histamine).
evidence: This is supported by prior research on histamine recycling.

claim: It was unclear how β-alanine is returned to laminar glial cells prior to this study.
source: This regenerated histamine is then repackaged into synaptic vesicles for subsequent light-induced release, but it is unclear how β-alanine is returned to the laminar glial cells (where it is needed to inactivate histamine).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: It was unclear whether β-alanine recycling is required for visual transmission prior to this study.
source: It is also unclear whether β-alanine recycling is required for visual transmission.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: High levels of β-alanine are detected in retinal pigment cells.
source: The finding that high levels of β-alanine are detected in retinal pigment cells suggested that pigment cells may be critical for the transport and storage of β-alanine in this system (Borycz et al., 2012; Chaturvedi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borycz et al., 2012 and Chaturvedi et al., 2014.

claim: Pigment cells may be critical for the transport and storage of β-alanine in the visual system.
source: The finding that high levels of β-alanine are detected in retinal pigment cells suggested that pigment cells may be critical for the transport and storage of β-alanine in this system (Borycz et al., 2012; Chaturvedi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior observations cited in Borycz et al., 2012 and Chaturvedi et al., 2014.

claim: BalaT is a plasma membrane transporter capable of transporting β-alanine into cells.
source: Here, we identified BalaT, which is a plasma membrane transporter capable to transporting β-alanine into cells.
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays in HEK293T and S2 cells shown in Figure 1A-B and localization data in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted photoreceptor synaptic transmission.
source: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted photoreceptor synaptic transmission, phototaxis behaviors, and contents and retinal distribution of β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted phototaxis behaviors.
source: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted photoreceptor synaptic transmission, phototaxis behaviors, and contents and retinal distribution of β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted β-alanine contents.
source: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted photoreceptor synaptic transmission, phototaxis behaviors, and contents and retinal distribution of β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted retinal distribution of β-alanine.
source: Mutations in the balat gene disrupted photoreceptor synaptic transmission, phototaxis behaviors, and contents and retinal distribution of β-alanine.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and F.

claim: BalaT expression in retinal pigment cells completely rescued the defective visual transmission of balat mutants.
source: BalaT expression in retinal pigment cells completely rescued the defective visual transmission of balat mutants.
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings of pdh-balat rescue shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The gap junction proteins Inx1 and Inx3 are required in retinal pigment cells for visual neurotransmission.
source: Furthermore, the gap junction proteins Inx1 and Inx3 were required in retinal pigment cells for visual neurotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings of Inx1/Inx3 double knockdown shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A novel β-alanine recycling pathway exists in which β-alanine released from photoreceptor cells is taken up and stored by retinal pigment cells.
source: We therefore provide evidence for a novel β-alanine recycling pathway, in which β-alanine that is released from photoreceptor cells is taken up and stored by retinal pigment cells, and then delivered to laminar glia via gap junctions, where histamine is inactivated by conjugation with β-alanine.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data from the study.

claim: β-alanine stored in retinal pigment cells is delivered to laminar glia via gap junctions.
source: We therefore provide evidence for a novel β-alanine recycling pathway, in which β-alanine that is released from photoreceptor cells is taken up and stored by retinal pigment cells, and then delivered to laminar glia via gap junctions, where histamine is inactivated by conjugation with β-alanine.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data from the study, particularly the Inx1/Inx3 knockdown experiments.

claim: Among ~600 putative transmembrane transporters encoded by the Drosophila genome, 20 head-enriched genes were identified as potential β-alanine transporters.
source: Among ~600 putative transmembrane transporters encoded by the Drosophila genome, we identified 20 head-enriched genes (Table 1) that represented potential β-alanine transporters (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis and is shown in Table 1 and Figure 1A.

claim: CG3790 exhibited β-alanine uptake activity when expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Only one candidate transporters, CG3790, exhibited β-alanine uptake activity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The β-alanine content of CG3790-transfected cells was approximately 119 Bq/mg, which was 2.7-fold greater than mock- or RFP-transfected controls.
source: The β-alanine content of CG3790-transfected cells was approximately 119 Bq/mg, which was 2.7-fold greater than measured for mock- or RFP-transfected controls (55 and 53 Bq/mg, respectively).
evidence: This is based on quantitative measurements from uptake assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CG3790 shares significant amino acid identity with the mammalian solute carrier family 22 (SLC22), including mouse and human OCT3.
source: CG3790 shares significant amino acid identity with the mammalian solute carrier family 22 (SLC22), which includes both mouse and human OCT3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The β-alanine transporting activity of CG3790 was confirmed in S2 cells.
source: The β-alanine transporting activity of CG3790 was further confirmed in S2 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays in S2 cells shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mouse GAT3 efficiently takes up β-alanine.
source: Mouse GAT3 (GABA transporter type 3), which is known to efficiently take up β-alanine, exhibited levels of β-alanine transporting activity that were similar to CG3790, suggesting that CG3790 is a bona fide β-alanine transporter (Christiansen et al., 2007) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Christiansen et al., 2007 and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CG3790 exhibited levels of β-alanine transporting activity similar to mouse GAT3.
source: Mouse GAT3 (GABA transporter type 3), which is known to efficiently take up β-alanine, exhibited levels of β-alanine transporting activity that were similar to CG3790, suggesting that CG3790 is a bona fide β-alanine transporter (Christiansen et al., 2007) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CG3790 does not exhibit histamine uptake activity.
source: Histamine uptake assays revealed that CG3790 does not exhibit histamine uptake activity.
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Human OCT2 exhibits histamine transport activity when expressed in S2 cells.
source: As a control, the human Organic Cation Transporter (OCT2), which is known to take up histamine, exhibited high levels of histamine transport activity when expressed in S2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CG3790 does not exhibit GABA transporting activity when expressed in S2 cells.
source: While mGAT3 efficiently transported GABA, CG3790 did not exhibit GABA transporting activity when expressed in S2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: mGAT3 efficiently transported GABA.
source: While mGAT3 efficiently transported GABA, CG3790 did not exhibit GABA transporting activity when expressed in S2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by uptake assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Flag-tagged CG3790 localizes exclusively to the plasma membrane when expressed in S2 cells.
source: Moreover, when we expressed Flag-tagged CG3790 in S2 cells the Flag signal localized exclusively to the plasma membrane (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CG3790 encodes a plasma membrane β-alanine transporter.
source: These data suggest that CG3790 encodes a plasma membrane β-alanine transporter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the uptake assays and localization data.

claim: CG3790 mRNA transcripts were absent from fly bodies.
source: As is seen with other eye-specific genes including ninaE (neither inactivation nor afterpotential E), which is expressed exclusively in photoreceptor cells (O'Tousa et al., 1985), and pdh (pigment-cell-enriched dehydrogenase), which is expressed exclusively in retinal pigment cells) (Wang et al., 2010), CG3790 mRNA transcripts were absent from fly bodies (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: CG3790 transcript levels were greatly reduced in the heads of GMR-hid flies.
source: Similarly, CG3790 transcript levels were also greatly reduced in the heads of GMR-hid flies, suggesting that CG3790 is primarily expressed in the fly compound eye (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: CG3790 is primarily expressed in the fly compound eye.
source: Similarly, CG3790 transcript levels were also greatly reduced in the heads of GMR-hid flies, suggesting that CG3790 is primarily expressed in the fly compound eye (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the qPCR data comparing wild-type and GMR-hid flies.

claim: CG3790 encodes a retina-enriched plasma membrane β-alanine transporter.
source: These findings indicate that CG3790 encodes a retina-enriched plasma membrane β-alanine transporter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and functional data.

claim: The gene CG3790 was named balat (beta-alanine transporter).
source: We therefore named this gene balat (beta-alanine transporter).
evidence: This is a nomenclature decision based on the functional characterization.

claim: Two null mutations in the balat gene were generated by deleting ~900 bp and ~660 bp genomic fragments using CRISPR-Cas9.
source: To study the function of BalaT in visual perception, we generated two null mutations in the balat gene by deleting ~900 bp and ~660 bp genomic fragments using the CRISPR-associated single-guide RNA system (Cas9) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 2A and PCR confirmation in Figure 2B.

claim: PCR amplification confirmed that the balat locus is disrupted in balat1 and balat2 flies.
source: PCR amplification of the balat locus from genomic DNA isolated from wild-type, balat1, and balat2 flies revealed a truncated balat locus in the mutant samples. Thus, the balat locus is disrupted in balat1 and balat2 flies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: balat mutations did not cause lethality or other visible phenotypes.
source: These balat mutations did not cause lethality or other visible phenotypes, so we performed electroretinogram (ERG) recordings to determine whether BalaT functions in phototransduction.
evidence: This is an observation from the generation and maintenance of balat mutant flies.

claim: Exposing wild-type flies to light results in a sustained corneal negative response and 'on' and 'off' transients in ERG recordings.
source: Exposing wild-type flies to light results in two primary components in the ERG recording, including a sustained corneal negative response resulting from photoreceptor depolarization, and 'on' and 'off' transients resulting from postsynaptic neuronal activity in the optic lamina (downstream of the photoreceptors) (Wang and Montell, 2007) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang and Montell, 2007 and ERG data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sustained corneal negative response in ERG recordings results from photoreceptor depolarization.
source: Exposing wild-type flies to light results in two primary components in the ERG recording, including a sustained corneal negative response resulting from photoreceptor depolarization, and 'on' and 'off' transients resulting from postsynaptic neuronal activity in the optic lamina (downstream of the photoreceptors) (Wang and Montell, 2007) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang and Montell, 2007.

claim: 'On' and 'off' transients in ERG recordings result from postsynaptic neuronal activity in the optic lamina.
source: Exposing wild-type flies to light results in two primary components in the ERG recording, including a sustained corneal negative response resulting from photoreceptor depolarization, and 'on' and 'off' transients resulting from postsynaptic neuronal activity in the optic lamina (downstream of the photoreceptors) (Wang and Montell, 2007) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang and Montell, 2007.

claim: Mutations in genes that disrupt histamine recycling exhibit reduced 'on' and 'off' transients.
source: Mutations in genes that disrupt histamine recycling exhibit reduced 'on' and 'off' transients, reflecting defective synaptic transmission of photoreceptors (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Both balat1 and balat2 mutant flies lacked ERG 'on' and 'off' transients.
source: Similarly, both balat1 and balat2 mutant flies lacked ERG 'on' and 'off' transients, indicating that BalaT is required for visual synaptic transmission (Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: BalaT is required for visual synaptic transmission.
source: Similarly, both balat1 and balat2 mutant flies lacked ERG 'on' and 'off' transients, indicating that BalaT is required for visual synaptic transmission (Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of ERG transients in balat mutants.

claim: The GMR-balat transgene completely rescued the 'on' and 'off' transients when crossed into balat1 mutant flies.
source: The GMR-balat transgene completely rescued the 'on' and 'off' transients when crossed into the balat1 mutant flies (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutations in the white gene affect histamine levels.
source: Mutations in the white gene, which encodes an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter, has been reported to affect histamine levels (Borycz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borycz et al., 2008.

claim: 'On' and 'off' transients were still absent in w+; balat1 flies.
source: To make sure that the white mutation was not affecting ERG phenotypes exhibited by balat mutants, we crossed the balat mutation into a wild-type white (w+) background and found that 'on' and 'off' transients were still absent in this w+; balat1 fly (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Disrupting visual transmission results in blindness, which is reflected in the loss of phototaxis behavior.
source: Disrupting visual transmission results in blindness, which is reflected in the loss of phototaxis behavior (Behnia and Desplan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Behnia and Desplan, 2015.

claim: balat mutant flies exhibited impaired phototaxis.
source: Consistent with the loss of 'on' and 'off' transients, balat mutant flies exhibited impaired phototaxis, which was fully restored by the GMR-balat transgene (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The GMR-balat transgene fully restored phototaxis in balat mutant flies.
source: Consistent with the loss of 'on' and 'off' transients, balat mutant flies exhibited impaired phototaxis, which was fully restored by the GMR-balat transgene (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BalaT is involved in visual transmission and the loss of BalaT severely disrupts vision.
source: These results strongly support the conclusion that BalaT is involved in visual transmission and that the loss of BalaT severely disrupts vision.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ERG and phototaxis data.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing was used to introduce mCherry into the balat locus downstream of the native balat promoter.
source: As we were unable to generate a high affinity antibody against BalaT, we used CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing to introduce mCherry into the balat locus, downstream of the native balat promoter (balat-mcherry) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: balat-mcherry flies were identified through PCR and RFP immunofluorescence.
source: We identified balat-mcherry flies though PCR and RFP immunofluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Homozygous balat-mcherry flies displayed the loss of 'on' and 'off' transients.
source: Importantly, homozygous balat-mcherry flies displayed the loss of 'on' and 'off' transients, as expected, indicating the insertion of mcherry into the balat locus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mCherry signals in the balat-mcherry retina were predominantly detected in retinal pigment cells.
source: The mCherry signals in the balat-mcherry retina were predominantly detected in retinal pigment cells, as it overlapped with the PDH signal (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: No mCherry signaling was detected in wild-type flies.
source: No mCherry signaling was detected in wild-type flies (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The pdh-balat transgene fully restored 'on' and 'off' transients when crossed into balat1 mutant flies.
source: The pdh-balat transgene fully restored 'on' and 'off' transients and phototaxic behaviors when crossed into balat1 mutant flies, whereas expressing BalaT in photoreceptor cells failed to rescue these phenotypes (Figure 2C–E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The pdh-balat transgene fully restored phototaxic behaviors when crossed into balat1 mutant flies.
source: The pdh-balat transgene fully restored 'on' and 'off' transients and phototaxic behaviors when crossed into balat1 mutant flies, whereas expressing BalaT in photoreceptor cells failed to rescue these phenotypes (Figure 2C–E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Expressing BalaT in photoreceptor cells failed to rescue the ERG and phototaxis phenotypes of balat1 mutants.
source: The pdh-balat transgene fully restored 'on' and 'off' transients and phototaxic behaviors when crossed into balat1 mutant flies, whereas expressing BalaT in photoreceptor cells failed to rescue these phenotypes (Figure 2C–E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings and phototaxis assays shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: BalaT functions in pigment cells.
source: These results indicate that BalaT functions in pigment cells, and that pigment cells may play an important role in transporting β-alanine from photoreceptors to epithelia glial cells in the optic lamina.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Pigment cells may play an important role in transporting β-alanine from photoreceptors to epithelia glial cells in the optic lamina.
source: These results indicate that BalaT functions in pigment cells, and that pigment cells may play an important role in transporting β-alanine from photoreceptors to epithelia glial cells in the optic lamina.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the tissue-specific rescue experiments and localization data.

claim: A multicellular network involving laminar glia and pigment cells mediates long-distance recycling of histamine metabolites.
source: It has recently been reported that a multicellular network involving laminar glia and pigment cells mediates long-distance recycling of histamine metabolites (Chaturvedi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaturvedi et al., 2014.

claim: The transport of histamine metabolites relies on the gap junction protein Innexin 2 (Inx2) in glia.
